claims.text: By default, SQLite automatically checkpoints when a COMMIT leaves the WAL at 1000 pages or more.
claims.quote: By default, SQLite will automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size

claims.text: A zero or negative auto-checkpoint threshold disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.
Checkpoints initiated by this mechanism are PASSIVE . Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled

claims.text: PASSIVE mode checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers and may leave work unfinished.
claims.quote: Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: FULL mode waits for writers and readers on the latest snapshot, then checkpoints all log frames and syncs the database file.
claims.quote: It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file. This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending

claims.text: RESTART waits until readers use only the database file, ensuring the next writer restarts the log from its beginning.
claims.quote: This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning. Like SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, this mode blocks new database writer attempts

claims.text: TRUNCATE mode truncates the log file to zero bytes before a successful return.
claims.quote: it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: Overlapping readers can prevent all checkpoints from completing, causing the WAL file to grow without bound.
claims.quote: if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Attempting checkpoints during reader gaps can avoid starvation caused by continuously active readers.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: SQLite syncs the WAL before moving its content into the database, then syncs the database before resetting the WAL.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: With synchronous=NORMAL, a separate checkpoint thread can keep the querying and updating thread from blocking on a sync operation.
claims.quote: If an application therefore runs checkpoint in a separate thread or process, the main thread or process that is doing database queries and updates will never block on a sync operation.

claims.text: With synchronous=NORMAL, transactions may roll back following a power failure or hard reset.
claims.quote: The downside to this configuration is that transactions are no longer durable and might rollback following a power failure or hard reset.

claims.text: As the WAL grows, read performance deteriorates because time spent checking it is proportional to its size.
claims.quote: read performance deteriorates as the WAL file grows in size since each reader must check the WAL file for the content and the time needed to check the WAL file is proportional to the size of the WAL file.

claims.text: Frequent checkpoints can improve read performance by keeping the WAL small, while infrequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost across more writes.
claims.quote: To maximize the read performance, one wants to keep the WAL as small as possible and hence run checkpoints frequently, perhaps as often as every COMMIT. To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible

claims.text: A checkpoint records its progress in the wal-index and resumes from that point on its next invocation.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: SQLite normally recycles the WAL by overwriting it from the beginning instead of truncating it.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: A final checkpoint runs when the last database connection closes, after which SQLite deletes the WAL and shared-memory files.
claims.quote: When the last connection to a database closes, that connection does one last checkpoint and then deletes the WAL and its associated shared-memory file, to clean up the disk.

limitations: The supplied inventory names only SQLite, transactions, and write-ahead logging; exact existing coverage within those topics is unknown.
